rows.selection_reason: 1) Evidence/uncertainty: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero evidence about which modality, encoder, or fusion strategy is effective. The most fundamental uncertainty is whether multimodal fusion adds value over a single-modality baseline at all. 2) What this tests: config_012 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest meaningful RNA-only baseline—PCA introduces no learned parameters, single-profile avoids aggregation confounds, and omitting the image modality isolates RNA signal. It establishes a clean performance floor. 3) Why best under limited budget: A fast, well-understood baseline with minimal training confounds is the highest-information first experiment. It calibrates expected accuracy/F1, tells us whether RNA alone is competitive, and provides the reference against which all subsequent multimodal experiments must be judged. Without this anchor, any multimodal result would be uninterpretable. It is also computationally cheap, preserving budget for later, more complex experiments.

Evidence: We have only one completed experiment (config_012: RNA-only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → 48.5% acc), so uncertainty is high across all design axes. The most fundamental question for a multimodal profiling study is whether adding the image modality provides any signal beyond RNA alone. Question: config_002 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat fusion, no aggregation) is the minimal-change extension of config_012—it keeps the same RNA encoder, same profile setting, and adds only a standard image encoder (ResNet50) with the simplest fusion (concat). This directly isolates the contribution of image information. Why this is the best next experiment: If multimodal outperforms the RNA-only baseline, it justifies further investment in image encoder choice, aggregation, and fusion. If it does not, it redirects the search toward RNA-side improvements (encoder, multiprofile). No other single experiment reduces uncertainty about this core design decision as cleanly, and it avoids changing multiple axes simultaneously.

Evidence: config_002 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.527 acc vs config_012 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) at 0.485 acc, suggesting ~4% gain from adding image. However, with only two data points we cannot tell whether the image modality is genuinely contributing or whether the multimodal architecture's added capacity is the source of improvement. Question: config_051 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50, no aggregation/fusion) is the clean image-only baseline that matches config_002 on image encoder and profile setting while removing RNA entirely. If image-only approaches 0.52, RNA adds little and we should focus on image representation; if it drops substantially below 0.48, multimodal fusion is genuinely synergistic and we should invest in better fusion/aggregation. Why this is best: it isolates the single most important design question—relative modality contribution—with a one-variable change from config_002, and the answer will redirect the entire remaining search toward the modality or fusion strategy that actually matters, making every subsequent experiment more targeted under the tight budget.

Evidence: config_002 (multimodal, singleprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, concat) achieved 0.527 acc, beating RNA-only (0.485) and image-only (0.208), confirming RNA is the dominant signal and that adding image via concat provides a modest but real boost. However, we have only tested one fusion method (concat) in the multimodal setting. Question: config_006 is identical to config_002 except fusion changes from concat to weighted, making this a clean single-variable A/B comparison that isolates the effect of the fusion mechanism. Why best next: Under a limited budget, the most informative experiment is one that changes exactly one design axis from the current best result. The fusion method is a fundamental architectural choice that will determine how we combine the (dominant) RNA and (weak) image streams; knowing whether weighted fusion helps or hurts relative to concat directly guides all subsequent multimodal experiments and prevents us from carrying a suboptimal fusion forward into more complex multiprofile/aggregation settings.

Evidence: All four completed experiments use pca_n2000 for RNA and singleprofile. RNA is clearly the dominant modality (0.485 vs 0.208 image-only), and multimodal concat adds ~4 pts over RNA-only. However, PCA is a purely linear, untrained dimensionality reduction, and we have zero evidence about whether a learned RNA encoder (scvi_n200, scgpt) could substantially improve the RNA representation. Uncertainty: It is unknown whether the RNA encoder choice is a high-leverage design decision or whether PCA already captures most of the useful signal. This experiment (config_032: multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat) is a clean single-variable comparison to config_002 (same fusion, same image encoder, same profile setting; only RNA encoder changes from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200). If scvi_n200 substantially outperforms PCA, it tells us to invest in learned RNA representations going forward; if it performs similarly, PCA is sufficient and we should prioritize other axes (multiprofile, image encoder). Under a limited budget, isolating the RNA encoder effect on the dominant modality is the highest-information next step before committing to more complex multiprofile or fusion architectures.

Evidence: All five completed experiments use singleprofile; the multiprofile dimension is entirely unexplored. The best configuration so far is config_032 (multimodal, singleprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, concat) at 0.536 acc, showing that scvi_n200 slightly outperforms pca_n2000 and concat slightly outperforms weighted fusion. Question: Does extending the best-known single-profile setup to multiprofile with transformer aggregation yield a meaningful gain, or does the added complexity fail to help? This directly tests whether multiple profiles carry complementary information that a transformer can exploit. Why best next experiment: The profile setting is the largest unexplored design axis and could have a larger impact than swapping the image encoder (which contributes only ~4% over RNA alone). Config_023 extends config_032 minimally—keeping the proven scvi_n200 encoder, resnet50 image encoder, and concat fusion—while introducing multiprofile with the most expressive aggregation (transformer). If it succeeds, it opens a productive direction; if it fails, we learn that multiprofile does not help under current settings and can redirect budget toward image-encoder or RNA-encoder variants. This is the highest-information experiment available under the constraint that multiprofile necessarily requires an aggregation choice.

The largest performance jump in the study is config_023 (multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat → 0.688) vs config_032 (singleprofile, same encoders, no aggregation, concat → 0.536), a ~15-point gain. However, two variables changed simultaneously: profile setting (single→multi) and aggregation (None→transformer). Since transformer aggregation is only applicable to multiprofile, the key uncertainty is whether the gain comes from having multiple profiles per se or from the transformer's ability to model inter-profile interactions. config_041 (multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is a clean single-variable ablation: it keeps multiprofile and concat fusion identical to config_023 but replaces transformer with a simpler avgpool aggregation. If avgpool performs comparably, the multiprofile signal itself is sufficient and we can avoid transformer cost; if it drops substantially, transformer aggregation is specifically critical for combining profiles. This directly informs whether to invest further in transformer-based architectures or simpler aggregation schemes, making it the highest-information-use experiment under the limited budget.

The current best result is config_023 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) at 0.688 acc, showing that multiprofile + transformer aggregation is the dominant performance driver. In singleprofile, concat and weighted fusion were nearly identical (0.527 vs 0.523), but that comparison was made without multiprofile + transformer aggregation, where the interaction dynamics between modalities may differ. Config_015 is a single-variable change (concat → weighted) from the current best, making it a clean A/B test of the fusion mechanism in the strongest known setup. If weighted fusion helps, it provides a free improvement to the best configuration; if not, it confirms concat is sufficient and redirects the next experiment toward RNA encoder (scgpt) or image encoder (ViT) as the next lever. Under a limited budget, this is the lowest-risk, highest-clarity experiment to either exploit the current best or rule out a design choice before moving to larger architectural changes.

The current best configuration (config_015: scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, transformer, weighted; acc=0.713) establishes that multiprofile + transformer aggregation + weighted fusion is the dominant architecture. However, the RNA encoder has only been tested as scvi_n200 in this best setting. Since RNA is the dominant signal (RNA-only 0.485 vs image-only 0.208), the choice of RNA representation is the most consequential remaining design decision. Config_024 swaps only the RNA encoder to scgpt while holding all other factors at their best-known values (multiprofile, resnet50, transformer, weighted), giving a clean single-variable comparison against config_015. This directly tests whether a pretrained generative RNA model (scgpt) provides a richer representation than the variational autoencoder (scvi_n200) in the multiprofile regime. If scgpt matches or exceeds scvi_n200, it opens a new direction; if it underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 as the preferred encoder and can redirect exploration toward the image encoder or other factors. Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information, most actionable next step.

Evidence: The best-performing configuration is config_015 (multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, weighted) at 0.7131 acc. All high-performing runs use resnet50 as the image encoder, yet image-only performance is very low (0.2079), suggesting the image modality's contribution may be underutilized. The image encoder is the one major design axis not yet varied in the multiprofile multimodal regime. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l (a stronger, larger pretrained backbone) improve the best-known configuration? Why this is the best next experiment: config_001 changes exactly one variable (image_encoder) from the current best (config_015), keeping scvi_n200, transformer aggregation, weighted fusion, and multiprofile fixed. This cleanly isolates the image encoder effect. If it improves performance, it identifies the image modality as a bottleneck worth further investment; if it does not, it confirms the current image encoder is sufficient and redirects attention to other axes (e.g., RNA encoder or aggregation). This is a high-value exploitation step that tests a logically motivated extension of the strongest evidence without conflating multiple changes.
